title: Typhoon Dujuan Slams Japan, Prompting Evacuation Orders for Nearly Two Million
summary:
Nearly two million people in Japan were told to evacuate as Typhoon Dujuan battered the country on Monday, bringing winds of 130 kilometres per hour and gusts up to 194 km/h. Japan's Meteorological Agency had warned of an "imminent threat to life," though many warnings were later downgraded. The highest-level danger warning remained in place only for Oshima Town.

The storm knocked out power for more than 50,000 people, cancelled hundreds of flights, and suspended rail services. It struck during a five-day holiday, forcing the cancellation of several events. Concerts at the Rock in Japan music festival were called off, and the Tokyo Game Show cancelled its Monday programme. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi reportedly delayed her trip to the United States, where she was due to meet President Donald Trump and speak at the UN General Assembly, to monitor the storm's impact.

Dujuan is Japan's 25th typhoon this year. It formed amid what scientists call a "super El Niño" — a period of unusually warm ocean water in the Pacific. Warmer oceans give storms more energy, leading to higher wind speeds. A warmer atmosphere can also hold more moisture, which means these storms may bring heavier rainfall.

Research suggests Japan has become more exposed to destructive storms, though climate change is not thought to be increasing the number of storms globally. Some regions could even see fewer storms. However, the ones that do form are likely to become more intense on average.

Authorities have advised the public to keep checking weather information. Firefighters in Kanagawa prefecture received a call from a man who reported his house had been crushed by a landslide. A worker also fell into a bamboo thicket along with heavy machinery and was taken to hospital.
why_it_matters: For a 12-14 year old, this shows how climate risk actually reaches people: warning systems, evacuation orders and infrastructure decide who stays safe, and Japan's experience is an early look at the dangers facing coastal cities everywhere — including the ones students may live in one day.

background_read: Japan sits in the western Pacific, where warm ocean water feeds many of the world's tropical storms — the same kind of storm called a hurricane in the Atlantic, but given the name 'typhoon' in this region. Typhoon names are not random: they come from a rotating list agreed by regional governments, and 'Dujuan' (the name of an azalea flower) was contributed by China.

'El Niño' is a natural climate pattern in which the surface of the Pacific Ocean warms up; a 'super El Niño' is an especially strong one that weather services around the world watch closely. Japan's Meteorological Agency (the government body that issues the country's weather warnings, similar to the National Weather Service in the United States) can raise alerts to a life-threatening level when a storm is about to strike.

Scientists expect climate change to make the strongest storms windier and rainier even if the total number of storms does not grow — which is why Japan, a wealthy country with strong sea walls, evacuation plans and warning systems, is often studied as a test case for how coastal nations can adapt.

perspectives.description: They argue the system worked: the Meteorological Agency gave early, forceful warnings, nearly two million people were told to leave in time, and the highest danger level was narrowed to the one town that needed it most. From this view, mass evacuation orders are a sign of preparedness, not panic — even if the storm's worst effects miss.

They point out that warnings covering nearly two million people were later downgraded, which can create 'warning fatigue' — people stop taking alerts seriously if they keep being told to flee and nothing happens. Evacuating so many residents also disrupts work, school and travel, and costs a great deal.

Research suggests global warming is not increasing the number of typhoons, and some regions may even see fewer. But warmer oceans feed the storms that do form, so they tend to be more intense and carry more rain — meaning Japan's rising exposure is a story about storm strength and coastal development, not storm count.

If the strongest storms keep getting stronger, countries may need to rethink evacuation rules, harden power grids and rail lines, and invest in sea defences. Cutting greenhouse-gas emissions is the long-term fix, but adaptation — how societies live with the storms already locked in — is now an urgent, practical question.
